Chapter 7: Communicating Your Love Language to Others
So, you’ve figured out your love language—that’s a big step. But here’s where things really start to change: when you share that insight with the people around you. Open, honest conversations are like a bridge, connecting what you know about yourself to the kind of connection you want with others. It’s about inviting someone into your world, and handing them the keys to loving you in a way that truly matters.
Think for a moment about your closest relationships. Ever felt misunderstood, or maybe a little invisible? Most of the time, that comes from things left unsaid—expectations we never voice, or assumptions we just hope others pick up on. When you gently express your needs, you open the door to deeper understanding and real closeness.
So, how do you actually talk about your love language? Here are some friendly, low-pressure ways to start:
You might share a story, or give a little example of what makes you feel truly appreciated. Maybe you say, “You know, I always feel really close to people when we spend time together, even if it’s just running errands.”
And when someone naturally speaks your love language, let them know you noticed! Genuine gratitude goes a long way, and it encourages more of the same.
Try using “I” statements, so it doesn’t come across as criticism. For example, “I feel really supported when you help me out around the house.” That way, you’re sharing what matters to you, without making anyone feel like they’ve done something wrong.
And don’t forget to be curious about what matters to them, too. Ask open-ended questions—something like, “What makes you feel most cared for by your friends or family?”
It’s important to have patience and empathy. Not everyone’s going to get it right away, and that’s totally okay. The goal isn’t to force someone to change, but to create mutual respect and understanding.
Let’s say you’re at work, and your manager often gives public praise. But you? You feel much more valued by a quiet, one-on-one “thank you.” By sharing your preference in a respectful way, you help your manager see what really motivates you—and that leads to better support all around.
Over time, these small conversations can really change the culture of your relationships. They build a sense of safety and openness, where everyone’s needs are seen, and everyone feels honored. And that’s what emotional intimacy is all about—being truly known, and accepted for who you are.
